strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant gap: while existing OCR and document benchmarks predominantly focus on text extraction / visual perception where answers can be found verbatim in the image, OCR-Reasoning specifically targets multi-step reasoning over text-rich images.
The data curation and quality control framework is sound, involving human STEM annotators, multi-stage review, and annotation of both final answers and intermediate reasoning paths.

The experimental evaluation is extensive and up-to-date, testing an array of recent frontier models (OpenAI-o1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Doubao-1.5-Vision-Pro) as well as open-source vision-language and reasoning models (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Kimi-VL-Thinking, etc.).

The empirical findings provide actionable insights: multimodal grounding significantly outperforms OCR+LLM pipelines, current visual RL/reasoning models struggle to generalize to text-rich reasoning, and even frontier models achieve less than 50% accuracy on this benchmark.
weaknesses: The dataset size is relatively modest (1,069 Q&A pairs over 1,022 images across 18 sub-tasks, averaging roughly 60 examples per sub-task), which may limit the statistical granularity of fine-grained breakdowns.

The reasoning path evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge (Table 4) lacks detailed discussion: the prompt template, judging criteria, score distribution, and agreement with human judgment are not thoroughly documented in the main text.
Using Gemini-2.0-Flash as one of the paths to generate candidate reasoning chains risks introducing model-specific priors or biases into the reference reasoning paths.

There are several drafting errors and unfinished sentences: the Abstract ends abruptly with 'The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at '; on page 8, the text erroneously lists GPT-4o twice ('9.2% on GPT-4o, and 1.0% on GPT-4o'); and Figure 6 duplicates the subfigure label '(a)'.

strengths: Clear and timely motivation: Most existing text-rich image understanding benchmarks (such as DocVQA, ChartQA, OCRBench) primarily measure perceptual text extraction where answers can be directly matched in the image. The paper quantitatively illustrates this gap in Figure 1 (where >78% of answers in existing benchmarks are extractable verbatim, compared to only 2.3% in OCR-Reasoning), effectively demonstrating the need for reasoning-focused evaluation.

Comprehensive taxonomy: The benchmark establishes 6 core reasoning categories (Spatial, Numerical Analysis, Mathematical, Enumerative, Logical, and Multidisciplinary Knowledge) spanning 18 practical sub-tasks, offering structured categorization of reasoning demands in text-rich visual scenarios.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The paper benchmarks a broad and contemporary suite of models, including leading proprietary MLLMs (OpenAI-o1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4o, Doubao-1.5-Vision-Pro, Gemini-2.0-Flash), open-source MLLMs across various parameter scales (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3), and specialized visual RL models (VL-Rethinker, MM-Eureka).

Insightful empirical findings: The experiments yield useful findings for the community, such as the substantial performance drop when substituting visual images with raw OCR text, the struggle of math-oriented RL methods when transferring to text-rich reasoning, and the differential impact of chain-of-thought prompting across model architectures.
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale per task: With 1,069 total samples distributed across 18 practical reasoning tasks and 6 core abilities, each sub-category contains only a modest number of samples (averaging fewer than 60 instances per sub-task). This limits the statistical significance when analyzing granular sub-task performance.

Potential bias and contamination in reference reasoning paths: In Section 3.1, the authors note that Gemini-2.0-Flash was used to generate one of the reasoning trajectories, which was then scored and potentially selected as ground truth. Evaluating models—particularly Gemini itself—against reasoning traces partly produced by an LLM introduces risks of stylistic bias or artificial alignment.

Lack of validation for LLM-as-a-Judge reasoning evaluation: In Section 3.3 and Table 4, an LLM judge is employed to score reasoning paths. However, the manuscript does not provide evidence of human-LLM alignment, inter-annotator agreement, or specific judge prompt templates, leaving the reliability of the scores in Table 4 insufficiently validated.

Presentation flaws and incomplete details: The abstract ends with an unfinished sentence missing the repository link ('The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at'). Additionally, there are duplicate bibliography entries (references [52] and [53] are identical), and Figure 7 displays inconsistent language usage (game-theoretic logic reasoning is in Chinese while other tasks are in English).

strengths: Timely and well-motivated focus on shifting text-rich visual evaluation from simple perceptual extraction to multi-step visual and symbolic reasoning.

Well-structured taxonomy categorizing text-rich image reasoning into 6 core reasoning capabilities and 18 practical tasks, addressing scenarios spanning financial analysis, schedules, spatial relationships, and handwritten STEM problems.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking covering a wide array of recent open-source and proprietary frontier models (e.g., Doubao-1.5-Vision-Pro, OpenAI-o1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, and specialized reasoning/RL models).

Revealing analytical findings, highlighting that text-only OCR pipelines fall short compared to native visual processing and that current reinforcement-learning-tuned multimodal models still struggle with text-rich reasoning tasks.
weaknesses: Several presentation and rendering errors: the abstract terminates with an incomplete sentence ('The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at'), and mathematical expressions in Figure 3 and Figure 7 are blanked out (e.g., 'Define the function .', 'Determine that f(x) is an odd function because , implying...').
Pervasive font/ligature encoding artifacts throughout the text and figures where characters with ligatures appear as replacement symbols (e.g., 'quesons', 'spaal', 'muldisciplinary').

Under-specified methodology for the LLM-as-a-judge reasoning evaluation in Section 3.3 and Table 4: the exact judge model, prompt template, scoring rubric, and human correlation/agreement analysis are not clearly detailed.
Relatively modest dataset scale (1,069 QA pairs over 18 sub-tasks averages fewer than 60 questions per sub-task), which may limit the statistical significance of finer-grained task evaluations.
Minor inconsistencies in text descriptions, such as in Section 4.2 where CoT improvements are attributed twice to GPT-4o ('9.2% on GPT-4o, and 1.0% on GPT-4o, respectively').

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in multimodal evaluation: shifting from shallow perceptual/OCR extraction benchmarks (e.g., DocVQA, ChartQA) towards complex, multi-step cognitive reasoning over text-rich images.
Well-structured taxonomy spanning 6 reasoning categories (spatial, numerical, mathematical, enumerative, logical, and multidisciplinary) and 18 sub-tasks.
Provides dual annotations consisting of both final verified answers and step-by-step reasoning rationales.

Thorough empirical evaluation across a wide range of models, including proprietary models (OpenAI-o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash), open-source vision-language reasoning models, document-specialized MLLMs, and OCR+LLM baselines.

Insightful diagnostic analyses, such as isolating the value of visual layout compared to pure OCR text, examining the varying impacts of CoT prompts across different model architectures, and providing error categorizations.
weaknesses: Potential question ambiguity and annotation quality issues in some samples. For example, in Figure 8, the question asks 'How many animals in the picture do not have a backbone?', but the reference solution counts the invertebrate *classes/groups* (10) rather than depicted animal instances (which o3-mini counted as 18). Similarly, in Figure 6, phrasing such as 'If you have already bought X, and then want to buy Y and Z, how much will it cost in total?' can be naturally interpreted as the cumulative cost rather than the incremental cost.

Relatively modest dataset size (1,069 questions across 1,022 images). Spanning 18 practical tasks means some subcategories have relatively few samples (fewer than 60 on average), which may lead to high variance on fine-grained subtask metrics.

The LLM-as-a-judge protocol for reasoning process evaluation needs clearer operational details, such as the exact multi-dimensional scoring rubric, prompt design, and standard inter-annotator agreement metrics (e.g., Cohen's or Fleiss' Kappa) beyond raw average score comparisons.
Incomplete text in the manuscript: the repository URL at the end of the Abstract is left blank ('The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at').

strengths: Clear motivation and timely contribution: Existing text-rich benchmarks (e.g., DocVQA, ChartQA, OCRBench) primarily evaluate textual extraction and shallow perception where answers are directly present in OCR text (as demonstrated in Figure 1). The paper effectively identifies and addresses the gap in evaluating complex, multi-step reasoning over text-rich images.

Comprehensive taxonomy: The benchmark categorizes tasks into 6 core reasoning capabilities and 18 practical sub-tasks, providing a structured framework covering spatial, numerical, logical, mathematical, enumerative, and multidisciplinary domains.
Dual annotation structure: Annotating both the final answer and step-by-step reasoning chains allows for both deterministic answer verification and qualitative/process-level evaluation.

Extensive and up-to-date empirical evaluation: The study evaluates a broad range of models, including state-of-the-art closed-source reasoning systems (OpenAI-o1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.0-Flash), open-source reasoning models (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3), document-specialized MLLMs, and OCR + LLM pipelines.

Insightful experimental findings: The benchmark reveals that current state-of-the-art models struggle significantly (<50% accuracy), document-centric models fail on reasoning tasks (<15%), and visual layout remains indispensable over raw OCR extraction.
weaknesses: Dataset scale: With 1,069 question-answer pairs spanning 18 sub-tasks, each individual task has a relatively small sample size (~50-60 examples on average), which may introduce variance when analyzing fine-grained subcategories.

Potential ambiguity in question formulation: As illustrated in Figure 8, the question 'How many animals in the picture do not have a backbone?' is interpreted by the ground truth as counting invertebrate taxonomic groups/classes (10), whereas an advanced model (o3-mini) counted individual animal instances mentioned (18). Such semantic phrasing ambiguities can penalize models that reasoned correctly under an alternative, valid interpretation.

LLM-as-a-Judge protocol details: While the reasoning process evaluation is a good initiative, the specific rubric, scoring scale (e.g., whether scores in Table 4 are normalized out of 100), prompt template, and calibration details for the judge model are minimally documented in the main text.
Incomplete link in the abstract: The repository URL at the end of the abstract is left blank ('The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at').

strengths: Clear motivation and well-identified problem: The paper clearly demonstrates through empirical comparison (Figure 1) that existing text-rich image benchmarks (e.g., DocVQA, ChartQA, OCRBench) primarily evaluate textual extraction and perception where answers are directly present in the OCR text, whereas OCR-Reasoning targets multi-step reasoning where answers must be derived.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors benchmark a wide array of state-of-the-art models, including text-only LLMs with OCR inputs, closed-source reasoning MLLMs (e.g., OpenAI-o1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet), general open-source MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3), and specialized document MLLMs.

Dual annotation format: In addition to final ground-truth answers, the benchmark provides curated step-by-step reasoning chains, enabling both deterministic accuracy evaluation and process-level analysis (using LLM-as-a-judge validated against human judgments).

Valuable empirical findings and ablations: The experiments reveal that vision cannot be trivially replaced by off-the-shelf OCR text, that current document-specialized MLLMs struggle significantly with multi-step reasoning (<15% accuracy), and that naive CoT prompting can degrade performance on models already trained with reinforcement learning (e.g., VL-Rethinker).
weaknesses: Dataset scale: The benchmark comprises 1,069 samples over 1,022 images. While comparable to some reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MathVista), this remains relatively modest across 18 distinct task categories (~60 examples per sub-task), limiting fine-grained statistical significance.

Validation of LLM-as-a-Judge: The paper validates LLM-as-a-judge by reporting aggregate average scores across four models compared to human evaluation, but lacks sample-level agreement metrics (such as Pearson/Spearman correlation or Cohen's kappa) between human evaluators and the LLM judge.

Minor presentation and formatting defects: In the abstract, the URL placeholder is abruptly left empty ('available at'). On page 16 (Section A.4), there is an incomplete dangling sentence ('made the same error as DouBao-1.5-Vision-Pro.').
